title: Bhadkeswar Temple
text: On new year’s day I was at Bhadkeswar temple in Dwarka, one of the ancient and prosperous cities believed to have been the capital of Lord Krishna's kingdom on the shore of the Arabian sea. I was 21 and yearning. I found a young woman probably my age or younger begging near the stone steps of the mandir, her beautiful face quietly peeking through the sheer green dupatta, two children clinging onto her. I brought myself on the edge of the stone wall with my legs dangling above the raging waves and sobbed. My long-lost life was siphoned out of me. In my mind were the unfocused ideas of what I previously considered myself collapsing into one, my true nature investigated and dissolved by a single glance, and the womb of my agitation torn apart to birth god. In another timeline I once lay at her feet. She looked at me with supreme knowledge and no desire. Then, three other children ran down the steps to meet her, prancing around her fondly, and as she lifted her arm a baby appeared nursing under her dress. Another world would already call her death. I walked up the stairs to the small street vendor and asked for five bowls of cut green mangoes with chili powder and five coconuts for her family. The sea breeze teased my hair and as I turned away I locked eyes with a small girl, maybe seven or eight with grey-blue eyes, sunkissed caramel skin, and knotted hair gallivanting about, a treasurer of eternal freedom and joy. She knew my secret and sensed my longing– she knew I was once free. She ran down the stone steps towards the sea, met her mother, and glanced back at me and waved. I brought the mangoes and the coconuts and placed them on the steps, held her hand, and prayed for her. I’ve never ever done that before. The waves swelled and slammed against the rock. All of our feet are wet.

title: Parallel Existence
text: 29 years ago I jumped to a parallel existence after a near death experience. Let me start by saying this will be long. My heart is already beating fast telling this story. Only those closest to me know that this happened until now. When I was 25 years old I was driving home from work one night. I lived in Los Angeles at the time. I was driving on Sunset Boulevard heading west towards my apartment in Brentwood. For those that are not familiar with the area there is an expanse of Sunset, near UCLA, that is very curvy. It is 2 lanes on either side with no shoulder. It was 8:30 on a Saturday night so there was some traffic. I was driving along and all of a sudden about 50 feet in front of me I saw a car but I was looking at the passenger door. A car had spun out of control and was perpendicular in my lane. I didn't have time to stop. I looked to my right and saw there was a car next to me so I had nowhere to go. I instinctively turned my car all the way to the right anyway. Once I had cleared the first car I spun it all the way to the left still trying to avoid the 2nd car. While all of this was happening I remembered a time with my mom at Disneyworld when I was 3. This is not a memory I have ever had. I vaguely remember parts of that trip but this memory was not one of them. I realized then that my life was flashing before me and I was going to die. I had never been so sure of anything. Every part of me knew I was about to die. I started screaming, to this day I don't know if I vocalized anything or it was all in my head. I yelled "No, no this isn't fair. I'm not done yet", all the while swerving all over Sunset Blvd. I suddenly stopped my car and I was now perpendicular in the opposing lane of traffic. I looked around and there was not a single car anywhere. It was like everything had been wiped clean. I put my car in reverse and proceeded home. I did not see a single car the rest of the way. I was only 5 minutes away from home at that point but Sunset Blvd on a Saturday night was completely empty. I got to my apartment and parked on the street. I didn't see one person. While walking to my apartment I came to the conclusion that I had died and because I said "No" I was stuck in some limbo. I had never wanted my roommate to be home so badly, unfortunately she wasn't. I called one of my best friends and said, "I need to ask you some questions. Please just answer me and I will explain after". I asked her my name, my age, what city we lived in and the date. Obviously she was very alarmed. I explained that I thought I was dead and I wasn't sure I was really on the phone with her. She tried to convince me that I was alive and that everything was okay. There was no way mathematically to escape it. There was nowhere for the car on the right to go. This moment has haunted me my whole life. There have been times when I have questioned my existence. I've wondered if my "life" since has been a very detailed death trip and I'm actually lying on Sunset Blvd bleeding out. After many years of meditation, spiritual practice and belief in quantum physics, I wonder what life I jumped into.

title: Secret Garden
text: i was, for once, feeling before thinking. i just let it all come over me. and i couldnt even feel it fully, but i was just crying and crying. there was a separation between my inward and outward self and my outwards self was expressing things my inward self could not explain nor understand. once i calmed down a bit, i walked down the bridge and through the rest of the trail. finally, i reached a walkway that cut into the quaint little neighborhoods right across sam's house. as i get through the walkway, i feel the most unstable but i also feel that divine voice telling me to stay calm. i cry more, feel more, realize more. as i walk up the hill and the sun beams over my face as i get into the neighborhood, i start to feel my feet steadying and my back straightening and the world sort of weaving around me-- i am a bouncing pebble in a pond, making waves, establishing itself. i dont feel fear, just calm. i start to smile and look around, noticing the hedges and flowers and cottages. i walk past a small church and hear a woman searching for a child in a gentle desperation. i keep walking and walking and walking and im in the most peace i've ever been. i notice myself and am aware of my energy. then, i reach an abandoned house with the flowers growing all over. i notice the vibrance of my sweater. then i reach an abandoned house and right across, i see a strange entrance into a small garden type thing. its like a secret garden lined with hedges and red benches and you can see the trees beyond. The divine voice was the strongest here, and this time i cried harder than i ever did. again, this is the first time i felt something before thinking about it. i looked up at the sky and felt i talked to god and asked it to reveal itself. i closed my eyes and found myself. it is me, the bearer of my perspective. i felt my ancestors in my blood. i know i can possibly have psychic/medium/esp - esque abilities if i opened myself up to that. but anyway my mental state in the secret garden was incredible. i felt so comfortable with myself and realized its not only the energy of the "outside" that i am afraid of but it really is my own foreign nature i had no idea how to cope with. i could so easily identify my inner instability. when i finally decided i'm ready to exit the garden (and it took a couple of tries), i somehow made it back to seventh street.

title: Snow Farm Dream
text: My best friend took me to some farmland during a time when it was covered in a thick layer of snow, gave me a large squirt gun, and told me to spray the cows as they came in. I take one look at the cows, and I get sad, and throw the gun into the snow. The farmer, or a farmhand, sees us, yells and curses at us, and makes us line up against the fence. I swear to him that it was all my friend's idea. This large mob of people consisting of everyone I know gathers around to watch this unfold, and at some point, my friend says something to me. In that moment, I fly into this murderous rage, grabbing him by the throat and screaming, "YOU SON OF A BITCH! I'LL FUCKING KILL YOU! FUCK YOU! FUCK YOU!" His face is getting redder and redder with every squeeze. Finally, my mom pulls me away, and I let him go.

title: Grown Woman
text: I am a grown woman now. [I don’t know what either of these things mean- to be grown and to be a woman]. Yesterday I was a child and once a girl, and yesterday no longer exists and never really existed. There’s always today. Anyway, I am supposed to be a grown woman today who does objective things. I have been told by many that I must decouple myself from my thoughts and reduce myself so I find solace in simple truths. [I am angry because I’m doing everything wrong]. I am a grown woman who stays neutral in expression. I am a grown woman who shares a natural cartesian partition between the world and herself. [Sadly, the observer must precede the observed]. I am a grown woman who has a lot of people that can fix me [everybody is broken]. I just need an Atheist’s guide to navigating grief and hope in the 21st century. And a guide for people who accidentally convince themselves that they have lived a different life altogether in their memory. And a guide for people who wrongly expect they’ve reached the limit to suffering. And a guide for what to do when you anticipate suffering because you’ve enjoyed too much. My expectations close the world for me. I don’t want to grow as an adult who is afraid. But I will never be afraid, and that scares me.

title: Observers and Admirers
text: Perhaps all along you wished you could transform intrapersonal to interpersonal without another body watching you, dreaming of you, admiring you. Captivation is in many ways a chase, a game of selfishness- a chase where you turn back and see nobody but your own reflection on the puddles of rainwater collecting on the pavement. You become increasingly elusive to everyone else just to attract the attention of a fictitious subject; a prized commodity, the apparent end to loneliness. Hence you idolize them as though they yield aesthetic interest and surface level captivation. This captivation wilts slowly over time to fibrous threads of a fantasy. Then what? The vision of them withers, you recreate them to be judgemental. You make sure to routinely utter the desperation you have in regards to their eviction from your soul. But when they leave, what must you do with yourself? Create a new subject that assesses you on a reasonable basis? Like what? Perhaps one that shares a love of Taoism and polo crewnecks? Give it a few months and your desires may morph into another. Eventually you might habituate the creation of an infinite supply of “observers” and “admirers” within your conscience. Soon the disillusionment will collapse when both subject and object must finally face each other and converge; when it is no longer ethical to behave elusively in a dire situation. When a loved one is suffering, when you are broken and in pain, whatever you do will never impress the subject of your creation because they are really just you in a pathetic painted shell of someone different.

title: The Hospital Vending Machine
text: At 2:13 in the morning, the hospital hallway looked less like a place for healing and more like a place where time had been forgotten. The vending machine hummed beside me with its rows of chips, candy bars, and bottled teas glowing like small artificial promises. My father was asleep in the room behind me, or pretending to be asleep. Earlier, he had asked me whether the trees outside still had leaves, even though the window faced a brick wall. I put two dollars into the machine and pressed the wrong number. A packet of sour gummy worms fell instead of the crackers I wanted. For some reason, that mistake almost broke me. I stood there holding the candy in my hand and thought about every small error that had led us here: missed appointments, delayed calls, the way everyone says “it’s probably nothing” until suddenly it is something. A nurse passed by and smiled at me gently, not with cheerfulness but with recognition. I sat on the floor under the vending machine light and ate the sour candy one worm at a time. Each one made my jaw ache. I remember thinking that grief did not arrive like a storm. It arrived like fluorescent light, like sugar on your fingers, like being awake when the whole building wanted you to be quiet.

title: The Neighbor’s Violin
text: Every evening at six, the neighbor upstairs practiced violin badly. Not charmingly badly, not in the way children are bad at things before becoming wonderful, but with a stubborn, sawing devotion that made the whole ceiling tremble. At first I hated her. I would sit at my desk and wait for the first note to split open the room. Then winter came, and the apartment building became a kind of ship. Pipes knocked in the walls. People carried groceries up the stairs with wet shoes. The radiator hissed under the window. At six, the violin began again, thin and wavering, always trying to become the same song. One night, during a snowstorm, the power went out. The building fell into a silence so complete that I could hear someone coughing three floors below. Then, from above, the violin started. No accompaniment, no light, no confidence. Just that same broken melody moving through the dark. I stood in the middle of my kitchen and listened. For the first time, I heard not noise but effort. The notes missed their mark, slipped, recovered, tried again. I never learned her name, but after that night I stopped resenting her. She was not ruining the silence. She was keeping it company.

title: Inventory of a Childhood Drawer
text: Inside the drawer were three marbles, a library card with the wrong address, a dried-up glue stick, two friendship bracelets, and a plastic dinosaur missing one leg. There was also a birthday candle shaped like the number eight, although I could not remember which birthday cake it had belonged to. My mother wanted me to throw the whole drawer away. She stood in the doorway with a trash bag and said, “You don’t need any of this.” She was right in the ordinary sense. None of it was useful. The bracelets were too small. The glue stick had no glue. The dinosaur could not even stand. But I kept touching each object as if it had a temperature. The blue marble had once been treasure. The library card had once made me feel independent. The broken dinosaur had survived a move, a basement flood, and at least two versions of who I thought I was. I threw away the glue stick first because it was easiest. Then the candle. Then nothing else. My mother sighed but did not argue. After she left, I placed the remaining objects back in the drawer, not because I needed them, but because they seemed to be holding open a door I was not ready to close.

title: The Wrong Funeral
text: I arrived at the funeral home twenty minutes early and realized almost immediately that I did not recognize anyone. The photograph near the entrance showed an old man with silver hair and a fishing vest. My aunt’s friend, the woman I had come to mourn, had been small, sharp, and almost always wearing red lipstick. I had entered the wrong service. I should have left, but a woman near the guest book touched my arm and said, “Thank you for coming.” Her face was so tired that correction felt cruel. I signed my name in handwriting that looked guilty. Then I sat in the back row and listened to strangers describe a man named Walter who loved lake trout, crossword puzzles, and telling the same joke twice. At first I felt ridiculous. Then, slowly, I began to feel implicated. Walter’s granddaughter cried while reading a poem. His son laughed and apologized for laughing. Someone said he never knew how loved he was. I stared at the carpet and thought: how many griefs are happening at any given moment, one room away from the grief we meant to attend? When the service ended, I slipped out before anyone could ask how I knew him. In the hallway, I found the correct room. Through the open door I saw my aunt waving me in. I stood between the two funerals for a moment, carrying one sorrow by mistake and another by obligation.

title: Instructions for Becoming Ordinary
text: First, choose a cup. Any cup will do, but it is better if it has no symbolic value. Pour the coffee. Do not think about the hands that picked the beans, the heat that changed them, the transport ships crossing dark water, or the fact that every morning is an agreement with repetition. Second, answer emails using phrases that make you sound intact. Say “No worries,” “Sounds good,” and “Just following up.” Do not mention that your dreams have recently become more coherent than your waking life. Third, walk outside. Notice the dog pulling its owner toward a tree. Notice the old man adjusting his cap before crossing the street. Do not turn these things into metaphors. This is very important. The ordinary world cannot survive being constantly translated. Fourth, when someone asks how you are, say, “I’m good.” Practice this until it becomes almost true. Fifth, return home. Put the cup in the sink. Let one object be only one object. Let the spoon be a spoon. Let the window be a window. Let the self sit quietly inside the body without demanding evidence. If this fails, begin again tomorrow. Most people are not ordinary by nature. They are ordinary by practice.

title: The Deer at the Gas Station
text: The deer was standing beside pump six as if waiting for someone to approve its credit card. It was late August, and the whole gas station smelled like asphalt, gasoline, and overripe grass. I had stopped there on the way home from a dinner where everyone talked too loudly about their plans. At first I thought the deer was fake. It stood perfectly still, one hoof lifted, ears turned toward the road. Then a truck pulled in, and its headlights washed over the animal’s body. It blinked. The driver got out, saw it, and froze too. For a few seconds, all of us — me, the driver, the cashier behind the glass, the deer — seemed caught in the same unfinished sentence. Nobody moved. Then the deer lowered its head and began licking spilled soda from the concrete. That was the detail that stayed with me. Not the strangeness of seeing a wild animal under fluorescent lights, but the humility of its thirst, the way it accepted sweetness from the ground. I wanted the moment to mean something clean: nature entering civilization, innocence among machines. But it was messier than that. The deer was hungry. The station was bright. I was lonely. The world had made a little mistake, and none of us knew how to correct it.
